title: No Drone Unturned: Ukraine’s Tech Scouts
content:
Ukraine, with limited manpower, needs asymmetric advantages wherever they can be found. Innovation is decentralized across many Ukrainian units, and across the country, volunteers, engineers, and soldiers are working hand-in-hand to develop new technology.

But there’s a limit to commanders’ capacity to withdraw soldiers from the front to train them on new kit or send them abroad to scout the best equipment for their needs, so foreigners are helping to bridge the gap.

Bryan Pickens, a former US Army Green Beret who has fought in Ukraine, says that any brigade with a premier drone unit also has tech scouts, while Ukraine’s defense intelligence agency (HUR) also has a group, including foreigners, scouting technologies abroad.

It’s a two-way street — Pickens, who carries out the role for Ukrainian special forces, said he is constantly being asked by Western companies to test their equipment in combat.

Obi, the callsign of a special forces operator from New Zealand who has been fighting in Ukraine since 2022, now spends most of his time evaluating emerging military technology. He works with defense companies and helps determine which systems can give Ukrainian forces an edge.

title: Russia Is Far from Defeated
content:
The phrase “quantity has a quality of its own” is often attributed (possibly incorrectly) to Joseph Stalin, and captures a persistent feature of Russian and Soviet warfare. Mass comes first, and everything else follows.

Vladimir Putin’s war on Ukraine has pursued the same logic. Moscow has tried to overwhelm Ukraine with more soldiers, weapons and the advantages of a far larger population, economy and defense-industrial base. This imbalance has forced Kyiv to improvise and find ways to compensate.

It has partly done so through innovative forms of asymmetric warfare, and its expanding drone and long-range strike campaign has hit Russian refineries, fuel depots, ports, ships and logistics sites far behind the frontline every single day for weeks. These attacks have disrupted fuel supplies, forced Moscow to divert resources to air defense and demonstrated that Ukraine can impose serious costs.

There is clear pleasure among Ukraine’s supporters at seeing Russia struck with such frequency and to such effect.

title: Russia’s Shadow War Surges Southward
content:
Russia’s shadow war against NATO allies has moved southwards, with three drone breaches of Romanian airspace in as many days, and a surge of other incursions in recent weeks.

Together with another attack on Poland, where a Russian cruise missile struck 100 km (62 miles) from the country’s eastern border on July 30, the incidents suggest that the Kremlin is once again turning up the dial to menace alliance members in the east.

Romania shot down the three suspected Russian drones on three consecutive days from July 24-26, a first for the NATO member. The Bucharest government’s response signaled a toughening of its reaction to airspace violation, and an unstated recognition that it is being tested by Moscow.

Romanian defense analyst Radu Tudor told this author Russia was “100%” to blame for the incursions. He suggested the firmer government response followed a Russian drone strike on a housing complex in Galați in May, when two people were wounded, and a fire started. “This was probably the trigger for the Romanian and NATO decision makers to engage and down those drones,” Tudor said.
snippet: Russia’s shadow war against NATO allies has moved southwards, with three drone breaches of Romanian airspace in as many days, and a surge of other incursions in recent weeks.
creator: Andrew Raynus

title: Generation Flee: Luring Home Ukraine’s Young
content:
“I’m done exploring the world. I don’t mind traveling, but I want to live in Ukraine,” said Oksana, a 25-year-old from southern Ukraine who has lived in Germany since 2022.

She has learned the language, found work, and secured stable housing, yet Germany still doesn’t feel like home. She misses the familiarity of Ukraine and the sense that, as a citizen, she can influence the society around her.

But she says she is not ready to return. Russia’s war is still raging, her home remains occupied, and she wants to pursue a master’s degree at a top university, establish herself professionally, and build a fulfilling life in a free and democratic country.

Her dilemma is part of a much larger problem. Ukraine urgently needs young people to sustain its recovery, economy, and already fragile demographic future, yet it is competing for them as they gain education, legal status, and professional experience in more prosperous and peaceful countries.
snippet: “I’m done exploring the world. I don’t mind traveling, but I want to live in Ukraine,” said Oksana, a 25-year-old from southern Ukraine who has lived in Germany since 2022.
creator: Andrew Raynus

title: Ukraine-Poland: Testing History to Destruction
content:
2026 is the Year of Jerzy Giedroyć. Americans may be forgiven for not recognizing one of Central Europe’s leading 20th-century democratic intellectuals, but Poles have no excuse.

The Polish Senate decided to honor him last year. Most of the country’s elite, including President Karol Nawrocki, a professional historian and former director of the Institute of National Remembrance, are aware of the man and his works.

Giedroyć (1906-2000) was the founder and editor of the influential Paris-based, anti-communist journal Kultura, which featured the writings of prominent Polish intellectuals and writers and served as a platform for the radically revisionist ideas about post-World War II Poland promoted by Giedroyć and his colleague, Juliusz Mieroszewski.

Their “doctrine” made two big claims. First, establishing good relations with Poland’s eastern neighbors and formerly Polish-occupied territories — Ukraine, Belarus, and Lithuania — was key to maintaining Polish independence in the face of Russian imperialism.
snippet: 2026 is the Year of Jerzy Giedroyć. Americans may be forgiven for not recognizing one of Central Europe’s leading 20th-century democratic intellectuals, but Poles have no excuse.
creator: Andrew Raynus

title: The West Must Confront China’s Biotech Offensive
content:
Chinese biotech companies have dramatically expanded out-licensing deals with global drugmakers, granting rights to their drugs nearly tenfold over the past four years, from $13.9 billion in 2021 to $137.7 billion in 2025. More than three-quarters of American pharma companies now depend on Chinese suppliers for at least some component of their drug manufacturing.

This dependence creates worrying security risks.

Yet Western policymakers and thought leaders seem deaf to the dangers. They preach careful engagement, “pragmatic risk management,” or joint venture structures to create “operational firewalls.”

“Don’t restrict Chinese biotech,” The Economist recommends. “Someone whose life is saved by a new medicine is unlikely to care whether it was invented at home or on the other side of the world.”

“Competition, not protections, is the answer,” added The Washington Post in a recent editorial.

title: We Need More Than a Ceasefire in Ukraine
content:
Why would Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, or any outside mediator, want to talk with Putin? Even if a ceasefire was achieved, as Serhii Plokhy argues in David and Goliath (Harvard Ukrainian Studies, February 2026), it would not bring lasting peace.

Neither side is content with the status quo. Russia cannot be satisfied with the Donbas rust belt for which so many have died, and Ukraine is acquiring the upper hand from its skillful use of military technology.

Putin wants Russia to retain Crimea and other lands occupied by Moscow’s forces in 2014 and after the 2022 full-scale invasion. He even demands the Donbas borderlands still controlled by Ukraine.

But Kyiv says such demands are off the table and wants Russia to return all the territory occupied since 2014 — including artifacts plundered from museums. A Russian-controlled Crimean peninsula cut off from its supply routes is not viable.

title: China Won the 5G Battle. Will It Win the 6G War?
content:
It was called the Clean Network initiative. The US jawboned European Union governments, and partners including Japan, India, and Australia, to remove Huawei and other Chinese vendors from their 5G networks, while laying the groundwork for similar restrictions in future 6G systems. 

But most governments across Latin America, the Middle East, sub-Saharan Africa, and Southeast Asia have not followed suit. Outside of North America, Huawei holds about 40% and ZTE about 14% of the telecom equipment market. 

Even in allied Europe, key countries such as Germany have resisted tearing out Chinese equipment, angry over US pressure and fearful of the cost. A new report from GSMA, a global trade body representing the telecom industry, estimates that the EU’s plan to rid its telecoms network of Chinese suppliers will cost up to €40 billion, four times more than initially estimated.

title: Russian Mass Mobilization? A Non-Denial Denial
content:
It has been a long time coming, but ordinary Russians are now experiencing a fraction of the horrors inflicted by their regime upon their neighbor. Now too, they’re hearing their state-directed media hint about a darker future of mass mobilization for the despot’s war.

Unlike Russia’s military, Ukraine’s armed forces are not targeting civilians, but everyday life is nonetheless impacted by the strikes against oil refineries, arms factories, online retailers, and warehouses. For the first time in 20 years, a majority of Russians say the economy is getting worse.

It is a sign of Kremlin paranoia that its men and women in the media note all this and begin to talk about a possible uprising, complete with references to 1917.

Even the most ardent cheerleaders of Russia’s war of aggression have to acknowledge what is happening as a result of Ukrainian long-range attacks, not least because the skies of Moscow and St. Petersburg are regularly blackened by smoke from burning buildings.

title: No Road Back to Putin, the Shakespearean Villain
content:
Thanks to Ukraine’s aerial offensive or logistical lockdown of Russia, Western observers have belatedly grasped that Ukraine both has cards to play and may also be turning the tide. All too predictably, this realization, especially in Europe, has fostered the idea that we have to talk to Putin.

Presumably Ukraine’s offensive, by precluding a Russian victory, facilitates or will make it possible to arrange a ceasefire. Likewise, these still undefined talks will also involve not just Russia and Ukraine but also Europe in equally undefined roles.

Sadly, the prevalence of such chatter (supported in recent months by the leaders of France, Italy and Finland) reveals that too many have not learned enough from Russia’s aggression. The belief that Putin will recognize his losses, cash in his chips, and seriously negotiate with either Europe, the US, or Ukraine rather than keep spinning the wheel betrays just how shallow is the understanding of Putin and Russia among Western elites. 

First, calls by Russians for the West to accept Moscow’s sovereignty, undoubtedly issued with the Kremlin’s assent, underscore the abiding strength of Moscow’s great power obsession (Derzhavnost’ in Russian).

title: Ukraine Is Failing Its Foreign Heroes
content:
We were sitting in a radio studio in central Kyiv, where an American volunteer soldier and I were being interviewed about the challenges faced by foreign troops.

As a Ukrainian veteran who sometimes helps them navigate these issues, I shared what I have seen from the inside, while he spoke from his experience serving in the Armed Forces as a foreigner. About 20 minutes into the conversation, the interviewer leaned forward with a question that caught me by surprise.

“Can I ask you something? Why don’t you just go home? Why are you — and so many others — still here?”

The soldier paused before answering.

“I can only speak for myself,” he said. “But I didn’t come to take from Ukraine. I came to protect freedom.”

It wasn’t a rehearsed line. It wasn’t meant to sound heroic. It was simply true.

He had been seriously wounded in combat. Almost everyone in his unit had been killed or wounded. Yet, years later, neither he nor most  of his comrades had received their UBD — the document confirming combat participation that opens the door to veteran status in Ukraine.
snippet: We were sitting in a radio studio in central Kyiv, where an American volunteer soldier and I were being interviewed about the challenges faced by foreign troops.
creator: Michael Newton
